analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal income tax code in 2013 and requires Congress to replace it with a new, simpler system.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended the federal income tax in 2012 without naming a replacement, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out the entire federal income tax code after December 31, 2012, and required Congress to approve a replacement tax system by July 4, 2012. The replacement is not written into the bill — the text only lists goals, such as a low rate for everyone, relief for working Americans, and no penalty on savings or marriage. It would also have taken a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate to delay the termination date. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest financial winners would be high-income households and investors, since ending the income tax removes the tax rates that fall most heavily on top earners and investment gains, and the bill's guidelines explicitly call for eliminating the tax code's 'bias against savings and investment'. Workers would keep paying Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, which the bill exempts from termination. The promised benefits for ordinary people — a simpler, lower-rate code — depended entirely on a future Congress writing a replacement that the bill did not itself contain.

how_it_helps.text: It terminates the Internal Revenue Code after December 31, 2012, meaning no federal income tax could be collected for any year starting in 2013.

It declares that any replacement tax system must apply a low rate to all Americans, provide tax relief for working Americans, eliminate the tax bias against savings and investment, and not penalize marriage or families.

It requires Congress to approve the replacement system in final form by July 4, 2012, and makes it much harder to postpone the termination date by requiring a two-thirds vote in both chambers to change it.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on whoever a future replacement system taxed, which the bill left undefined. If no replacement passed by the deadline, the federal government would lose its largest revenue source, threatening funding for everything from defense to Medicare. If the replacement shifted toward a consumption-style tax (as the guidelines suggest by eliminating the bias against savings and investment), lower- and middle-income households, who spend most of what they earn, would likely pay a larger share of their income in taxes than under a progressive income tax.

drawbacks.text: The bill ends the income tax on a hard deadline without actually replacing it — the new system is described only as a set of goals, not a written law — so if Congress failed to agree on a replacement by its own July 2012 deadline, federal income taxation would simply lapse.

It requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers to postpone the termination date, making it extremely difficult for any future Congress to delay or reverse the repeal even if the replacement system turned out to be unworkable or to raise far less revenue.

Ending the income tax would eliminate the federal government's largest revenue source — the revenue that funds defense, Medicare, Social Security payments, and interest on the debt — and the bill's guidelines point toward a consumption-style system that tax analysts generally find less progressive, shifting more of the tax burden toward wage earners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — a simpler tax code — is broadly popular, but the bill put the cart before the horse: it would have ended the current income tax on a hard date without any replacement written, and its own text named no actual tax to take over. If Congress had missed its deadline, all federal income taxation would simply lapse, which no serious tax writer supported. The two-thirds rule would also have made it very hard for a future Congress to fix the date even if the replacement plan failed. The cost of certainty about what happens after 2012 outweighed the symbolism.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: H.R. 982 was introduced on February 11, 2009, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Rules Committee.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action after the February 11, 2009 referrals; the bill died in committee at the end of the 111th Congress.
It had 116 cosponsors — 114 of the chamber's 178 Republicans and 2 of 253 Democrats — but no Democratic committee chair brought it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost or gained money, since the bill never advanced; the outcome preserved the existing income tax system, which continued to collect the revenue that funds federal programs. Opponents of scrapping the income tax without a written replacement were spared the risk of a revenue lapse.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax system continued unchanged

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Internal Revenue Code after 2012.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican — 114 of 178 House Republicans signed on versus just 2 of 253 Democrats — and no Democratic-controlled committee or floor action ever followed.

industries.note: Ending the income tax while 'eliminating the bias against savings and investment' would cut the top tax rates that fall most heavily on high earners and investment income. The replacement guidelines point toward a low-rate or consumption-style system, so the largest dollar benefits would flow to the wealthiest households.

Terminating the current code would shrink or force a wholesale retooling of the tax preparation, software, and accounting services built on the existing tax code. The bill's stated aim of simplicity would reduce demand for their services.

industries.industry: Payroll-funded social insurance (a preserved carve-out, not an industry)
industries.note: The bill explicitly keeps payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare intact even after the income tax ends, preserving those programs' funding while the rest of the tax code is scrapped. Ordinary workers' payroll contributions would continue, but the income-based financing that funds most federal spending would disappear.
